name: Illusory superiority
statement: On most desirable traits and skills, more people place themselves above the average person than the arithmetic allows.
meaning: The claim is about a distribution rather than about any one rating. Being above average is not an error, because somebody has to be. What the studies find is that the share of people claiming the position is larger than the share that can hold it, so the aggregate is wrong in cases where no individual rating can be shown to be. Svenson put the point in its sharpest form by asking for a position in a percentile ranking, where more than half of a group cannot sit above the median. The effect is defined across traits and skills rather than in one domain, and its size moves with which trait is asked about and how the question is worded.

origin.note: Svenson set out to replicate older claims, which he called poorly documented, that 70 to 80% of drivers put themselves in the safer half. He does not use the label "better-than-average effect" anywhere in the paper.

evidence: Svenson gave written questions to 161 licensed drivers. Eighty-one answered an advertisement in a University of Oregon student paper, median age 22, and 80 were psychology students at the University of Stockholm, median age 33. Each person judged either skill or safety, not both. Skill was judged by 41 of the Americans and 45 of the Swedes, safety by 40 and 35. Answers were marked on one of ten successive 10% intervals. The comparison group was the other people in the room, named in the question and set explicitly against Eugene, Oregon or against Stockholm and Sweden. On skill, 93% of the American sample and 69% of the Swedish put themselves above the median driver, and 46.3% of the Americans claimed the most skilful fifth. On safety the figures were 88% and 77%. No statistical test appears in the six pages, a point Koppel and colleagues make again when setting up their replication. Zell, Strickhouser, Sedikides and Alicke later pooled 291 independent samples from 124 published articles and 965,307 participants, and put the effect at dz = 0.78, 95% CI [0.71, 0.84]. Five samples supplied most of that total, two of them 805,708 participants between them, and dropping all five leaves 45,160 people across 286 samples, an average of 157.90 each. The six-figure total belongs to the collection rather than to the estimate. Their numbers here are read from the authors' accepted manuscript in the University of Southampton repository, the published version being paywalled.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication with 1,203 American drivers found the effect on all three response scales it tried.
replication.detail: Koppel, Andersson, Tinghög, Västfjäll and Feldman ran the study online in 2019 on American MTurk workers, moving the comparison group from people in the room to drivers in the participant's US state. Eighty-four people who said they held no licence were filtered out, and the 1,203 who remained were divided across three response scales. On Svenson's own percentile scale, 386 of 413 placed themselves above the median driver for safety, 95% CI [0.91, 0.96], and 370 of 405 did so for skill, [0.88, 0.94]. The paper's table gives the safety proportion as 0.94 where its running text gives 93%, on the same 386 of 413 participants. A seven-point Likert version gave Hedges's g = 1.39 for safety on 387 people and g = 1.19 for skill on 379, the figure in the field below. The third scale is the informative one. Adding an explicit 50% midpoint to the percentile categories left safety at 91% and dropped skill to 78%, because 14.6% of participants took the midpoint rather than a side. Intervals for the three skill measures overlap. For safety the Likert interval sits below the two percentile ones, which the authors read as a slightly smaller effect on that scale.

study.cite: Koppel, L., Andersson, D., Tinghög, G., Västfjäll, D., & Feldman, G. (2023). We are all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers: Successful replication and extension of Svenson (1981). Meta-Psychology, 7, MP.2021.2932.

limits: The comparison target does most of the work, and it need not be the self. Klar and Giladi ran eight studies in which participants judged an anonymous student, individuated in one version by nothing but an ID number, as better than the average student and above the group median. A ninth reversed it: an anonymous member of a highly disliked out-group was judged worse than that group's average member. Their reading is that people have difficulty comparing a singular target with a generalised one, and the effect was reduced when an enriched version of the average student was supplied. Giladi and Klar then found the same superiority and inferiority pattern in six experiments on objects and concepts, which they take as support for a cognitive account over a social one. Chambers and Windschitl argue in a review that ordinary information-processing limits can produce above-average effects with no motive to self-enhance. Those three papers are paywalled and were not obtained; what is said about them here comes from their abstracts at PubMed. Method moves the number. Zell and colleagues report dz = 0.91 for direct comparisons against 0.70 for indirect ones, 0.89 for personality traits against 0.51 for abilities, and 0.62 for the percentile method Svenson used. Publication bias is not spread evenly either. Egger's test was significant across all 291 samples, intercept 4.40, p < .001, and not significant once the five huge samples were dropped, intercept 0.77, p = .30. Under the most stringent selection model the pooled effect falls from 0.78 to 0.50, the percentile method from 0.62 to 0.21 and abilities from 0.51 to 0.09. Culture moves it as well. Across 11 studies measuring both groups, European Americans gave dz = 0.98 against 0.40 for East Asians, Q(1) = 6.02, p = .01. On individualistic traits the gap ran 1.20 against 0.41, and on collectivistic traits it closed to 0.96 against 1.03, p = .82. Kim, Kwon and Chiu offer a reading on which the wording does the work. Their 288 American undergraduates rated themselves against an average student, a typical student, or a student at the 40th, 50th or 60th percentile. On the eight general abilities, ratings against the average student, M = 4.79 on a seven-point scale, matched the 40th-percentile target at 4.86 and beat the 50th and 60th at 4.31, both p < .001. The percentile cells held 32, 39 and 39 people against 84 in the average condition. That account does not reach Svenson's question, which asked for a percentile position rather than a comparison with an average. The effect also reverses where absolute skill is low, which is the worse-than-average effect, entry no. 266. Kruger's abstract reports that cognitive load made both directions worse, and the preregistered replication of his study recruited 756 people and analysed 691.
misreadings: Svenson's figure travels badly. It is quoted as 93% of drivers rating themselves above average, when it was 41 American students rating driving skill against the other people in the room; the matching Swedish figure was 69%, and the safety figures were 88% and 77%. Above average and above the median are also different claims, and only the second is capped at half a group. The other figure quoted in this connection, usually with no document behind it, is the College Board's. Its 1976-77 Student Descriptive Questionnaire asked college-bound seniors to rank themselves against others of their age on 14 skills, and 828,516 answered at least one item. The national report gives 89% rating themselves above average on getting along with others and 70% on leadership, 74% among men and 66% among women, with 98% at average or better on leadership. This is not the Dunning-Kruger effect, entry no. 4, which asks whether poor performers in particular misjudge themselves. Illusory superiority is a statement about the whole distribution and predicts nothing about who is worst. It is not on its own evidence of self-flattery either, since Klar and Giladi's anonymous student was rated above average by people with no stake in him.
